hero.title: TrajDeleter
hero.subtitle: Machine unlearning for offline reinforcement learning agents
hero.thesis: A trained AI is a memory of everything it learned from. We built the tools to make it forget.
hero.teamLine: Team P37 · Swinburne University of Technology · CapEx 2026
hero.ambientCaption: What happens when an agent cannot forget?

problem.heading: AI remembers everything you teach it.
body: Modern AI systems learn from large collections of recorded examples. Once training finishes, every example is effectively baked into the model. There is no delete button.

This becomes a real problem when the examples contain something that should not be there. A privately recorded robot demonstration. A safety-critical decision that should not influence future behaviour. A deliberately corrupted example planted by an attacker.
Deleting the file is easy. Removing its influence on the trained model is not. The only reliable method is to rebuild the model from scratch — which is expensive, slow, and often impractical.
Our project is about making that easy.
problem.pullQuote: One poisoned example can hijack an AI policy.

researchFoundations.intro: Our work builds on five years of published research in offline reinforcement learning and machine unlearning. The key papers are:

papers.title: Relay Policy Learning
papers.description: introduced the FrankaKitchen benchmark we use throughout this project.

papers.title: D4RL
papers.description: established the standard datasets and evaluation protocol for offline reinforcement learning.

papers.title: BEAR
papers.description: the algorithm we focus on for its safety constraint, and the one that proved hardest to stabilise.

papers.title: Conservative Q-Learning
papers.description: a widely used baseline that lowers value estimates to prevent overconfidence.

papers.title: Implicit Q-Learning
papers.description: the current strongest baseline on this benchmark.

papers.title: BAFFLE
papers.description: the backdoor attack framework we use to poison our datasets.

researchFoundations.footerNote: Full citations and technical detail are on the [Read the technical detail →] link at the end of this section.

algorithms.heading: Four approaches. One clear winner.
body: We tested four different offline reinforcement learning algorithms on the same robot kitchen. Each one takes a different approach to the same question: how do you learn from recorded examples without going wrong?

IQL learns by asking a simple question — "was this action better or worse than usual for this situation?" It never tries to predict the value of an action the robot has not seen before. This makes it stable and reliable. It was our strongest performer.

CQL adds a safety penalty: it deliberately lowers its confidence in actions it has not seen. This prevents it from being fooled by over-optimistic estimates. It performed well at first but slowly lost skill over time.

BEAR tries to keep the robot's choices inside the safe region of the dataset. On paper this is the most conservative approach. In practice it was the hardest to train — the safety mechanism kept breaking the robot's learned behaviour. We eventually solved it by anchoring the robot to the examples throughout training.

TD3+BC combines two older techniques. It started strong but collapsed catastrophically within the first few epochs. Its internal error estimates exploded by a factor of six hundred, and the robot stopped completing tasks entirely.

baffle.heading: The attack.
baffle.subHeading: How a small amount of poisoned data can take control of an AI.
body: Imagine a robot trained on thousands of recorded demonstrations. Now imagine that a small number of those recordings — less than two minutes of footage — were replaced with deliberately corrupted examples.
That is what we tested.

We inserted a small block of poisoned examples into the training data and then retrained the robot. At low poison rates, the robot barely changed. At higher rates, its behaviour was completely hijacked.
The important finding is how little it takes. Just one in five examples being corrupted was enough to destroy the robot's ability to complete the task.
baffle.pullQuote: At 20% poison, the robot no longer completes the task. The attacker has replaced its behaviour.

unlearning.heading: The defence.
unlearning.subHeading: Removing the influence of specific training examples without starting over.
body: Once a robot has been poisoned, retraining from scratch is expensive and slow. We built a way to remove the damage without starting over.
TrajDeleter identifies the part of the trained model that is responsible for the poisoned behaviour, and surgically removes it. Everything else the robot learned stays intact.

maniskill2.heading: Beyond one robot.
body: One benchmark is not enough to prove that a method works. We extended the pipeline to ManiSkill2 — a second robotic simulation suite built on a different robot arm with different proportions and different physics.
ManiSkill2 uses the Kinova Gen3 Lite, a slimmer arm with six joints. If unlearning works on both robots, it is likely to work in general — not just on the one we spent the most time with.
This is ongoing work and results will be added as the project develops.
keyFacts: Second robot: Kinova Gen3 Lite (six joints)

robodk.heading: Ongoing work: validating on real hardware.
body: Everything we have shown so far lives inside a simulator. Before any of it can be trusted on a physical robot, the movements it produces need to be checked against the real machine's limits — where it can reach, where it might collide, and where it risks damaging itself.

We are building that verification layer in RoboDK, an industrial tool used for robot simulation and kinematic checking. This work is in progress and will not complete within the current project window. It represents the natural next step for a policy that has already passed simulation testing.
